plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle is the polar analogue of a Cartesian rectangle, defined by two constant-r circular arcs and two constant-theta rays; its constant-r sides are curved, which is why polar area carries an extra factor of r.
elements: origin point at lower-left
polar axis: horizontal black ray from origin (theta = 0 reference line)
inner circular arc r = 1.5, solid blue, centered at origin
outer circular arc r = 2, solid blue, centered at origin
lower ray theta = pi/6, dashed red, from origin
upper ray theta = pi/4, dashed red, from origin
shaded light-blue curved quadrilateral region R between the two arcs and two rays
label 'R' centered in the shaded region
label 'r = 2' near the outer arc (top)
label 'r = 1.5' near the inner arc (mid-left)
label 'theta = pi/4' near the upper ray (left)
label 'theta = pi/6' near the lower ray (lower-left)
overlay: straight-sided Cartesian rectangle outline (gray dashed) anchored at the inner corner with the same radial width and tangential extent, shown only when the overlay toggle is on

interactions.label: Inner radius r1
interactions.teaches: The inner boundary is a circular arc of constant r; moving r1 slides that arc radially while the angular width of R stays fixed, showing r1 is a radial bound, not an angular one

interactions.label: Outer radius r2
interactions.teaches: Together with r1, the outer arc sets the radial thickness of R; the gap r2 - r1 is the delta-r that appears in the polar integral limits

interactions.label: Lower angle theta1
interactions.teaches: The lower boundary is a ray of constant theta; rotating theta1 swings that ray about the origin while the radial bounds stay fixed, showing theta1 is an angular bound

interactions.label: Upper angle theta2
interactions.teaches: Together with theta1, the upper ray sets the angular sweep of R; the gap theta2 - theta1 is the delta-theta in the polar integral limits

interactions.label: Overlay straight rectangle
interactions.teaches: A true Cartesian rectangle with the same delta-r by delta-theta extent has four straight sides; laying it over R reveals that R's two constant-r sides bulge into circular arcs, so R is only an analogue of a rectangle and its area is not simply delta-r times delta-theta

demo_steps.title: The polar rectangle
demo_steps.narration: Region R is bounded by two concentric circular arcs (r = 1.5 and r = 2, solid blue) and two rays from the origin (theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4, dashed red). It is the polar counterpart of a Cartesian rectangle: two sides hold r constant, two hold theta constant.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the radial bounds
demo_steps.narration: Drag r1 and r2: the two blue arcs slide in and out and R thickens or thins radially, while the red rays and the angular width stay put. The radial extent of R is exactly r2 - r1.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the angular bounds
demo_steps.narration: Now drag theta1 and theta2: the red rays rotate about the origin and R sweeps through a wider or narrower angular sector, while the blue arcs keep their radii. The angular extent is theta2 - theta1.

demo_steps.title: Curved sides, not straight
demo_steps.narration: Reset the bounds and turn on the straight-rectangle overlay. The gray straight-edged rectangle matches R at the inner corner but R's outer arc bows beyond it: the constant-r sides are circular arcs, not straight lines. This curvature is precisely why the polar area element is r dr dtheta rather than dr dtheta.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A polar rectangle looks like a rectangle in (r, theta) space but its constant-r edges are circular arcs in the plane, so its true area grows with r — the geometric reason the polar double integral uses r dr dtheta.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the origin at the lower-left with a horizontal black polar axis extending right. Draw two concentric solid-blue circular arcs centered at the origin spanning the sector between the two angles; the inner arc is r=1.5 and the outer r=2. Draw two dashed-red rays from the origin at theta=pi/6 (lower) and theta=pi/4 (upper), extended a little past the outer arc. Fill the curved quadrilateral between the arcs and rays in light blue and label it R in italic serif. Position labels as in the source: 'r = 2' above the outer arc, 'r = 1.5' left of the inner arc, 'theta = pi/4' to the left near the upper ray, 'theta = pi/6' lower-left near the lower ray, all in italic math styling with pi shown as a fraction. The Cartesian overlay is a gray dashed straight-edged rectangle anchored at the inner corner (r1, theta1) whose horizontal side equals r2-r1 and whose vertical side equals the tangential arc length, drawn on top so the bulge of the outer blue arc beyond the straight top edge is obvious. Sliders should live-update the arcs/rays and the shaded wedge; clamp so r2 > r1 and theta2 > theta1.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for r1 and r2 (pre-filled 1.5 and 2): stretch or shrink the two bounding arcs and watch the curved quadrilateral R resize between them while the angular bounds stay fixed
- Sliders for θ1 and θ2 (pre-filled π/6 and π/4): rotate the two bounding rays and watch R sweep through the new angular extent while the radial bounds stay fixed
- Toggle to overlay a straight-sided Cartesian rectangle of the same Δr × Δθ dimensions at the same corner — shows why R is only an "analogue" of a rectangle: two of its sides are curved because r is held constant on a circular arc rather than a straight line
